analysis.investment_thesis: FIVESTAR is an NBFC — a category the Magic Formula explicitly excludes because borrowed capital is the raw material of the business, not a distortion to adjust for. Even if we force the metrics, earnings yield of ~7.4% (EBIT 1,505 Cr / EV ~20,360 Cr) falls well below my 12% minimum threshold, and ROIC is computationally meaningless when loans are the asset.
key_strengths: Exceptional revenue growth: 33%+ CAGR 2022-2025 (INR 1,233 Cr → 2,706 Cr) with net profit doubling in 2 years to INR 1,072 Cr
Focused niche: micro-entrepreneur small-ticket mortgage lending with 63.5% operating margins, implying pricing power and disciplined underwriting
Forward P/E of 11.1x is reasonable if FY2026 earnings deliver ~INR 1,254 Cr, suggesting limited downside from current valuation
key_risks: Financial company — Magic Formula explicitly excludes this; ROIC and earnings yield calculations are structurally distorted for lending businesses
Persistently negative OCF (0/5 years positive, -1,045 Cr in FY2025) — normal for NBFCs but means the business requires constant external capital and cannot self-fund growth
Debt tripled in 3 years (INR 2,559 Cr → 7,922 Cr), D/E at 1.23x; any credit cycle deterioration or funding cost spike compresses spreads immediately
red_flags: Financial company: Magic Formula does not apply — standard ROIC and EV-based earnings yield calculations break down
Promoter holding of only 18.56% is very low — limited skin in the game for the management team running a leveraged lending book

Trailing P/E of 88.9x is irreconcilable with Net Profit of INR 1,072 Cr and Market Cap of INR 13,935 Cr (implied P/E ~13x) — suggests a data quality issue or a large one-time item in the trailing period
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula applicability is near-zero here. Greenblatt's framework works by finding businesses that earn high returns on tangible capital purchased cheaply relative to EBIT. NBFCs break both sides of this equation: their "capital employed" is mostly borrowed money deployed as loans, so Net Working Capital + Net Fixed Assets tells you nothing useful about the engine of value creation. Forcing the math anyway, EV comes to roughly INR 20,360 Cr (Market Cap 13,935 + Debt 7,922 − Cash 1,497), and EBIT (using operating income) is INR 1,505 Cr, yielding an earnings yield of ~7.4% — well below my 12% floor for even a cursory look. ROIC on a balance sheet that is 55% borrowed loans makes no sense to compute.

On pure business quality (setting the formula aside), the company's 33% revenue CAGR and 16% ROE are respectable but not exceptional for a growth-stage NBFC with a clean book. The structural headwinds are real: every rupee of loan growth requires external debt, OCF has been negative all five years, and debt has tripled to INR 7,922 Cr. Promoter stake of 18.56% adds a governance concern. At a forward P/E of 11x, the market is pricing in continued strong growth with no credit cycle — a fragile assumption for an NBFC extending to micro-entrepreneurs. This is not a Magic Formula stock; it's a credit-cycle bet best left to NBFC specialists.
